questions.prompt: In a first conditional sentence, what does the if clause state?
questions.explanation: The if clause states the condition — what may happen — so the answer is "the condition". "the result" is the tempting mistake: the result belongs to the main clause, the one with will. The if clause gives neither a reason (that is because) nor the place and the time.

questions.prompt: Which sentence is a correctly formed first conditional?

options.text: If you will study hard, you will pass.
If you studied hard, you will pass.
If you study hard, you will pass.
If you study hard, you will passes.

questions.explanation: "If you study hard, you will pass." is correct: simple present in the if clause (study), will + base verb in the main clause (will pass). "If you will study hard" puts will in the if clause, the classic mistake; "studied" is the simple past, not the present; "will passes" adds an -s after will, where the verb must stay bare.

questions.prompt: Which tense follows "if" in the if clause of a first conditional?
questions.explanation: The if clause takes the simple present (If I want a tour…), even when the action is in the future. "the future with will" is the tempting answer, but will belongs only to the main clause; the simple past and the present perfect are not part of this pattern.

questions.prompt: In the first conditional, what is "won't" short for?
questions.explanation: "won't" is the short form of "will not": it makes the result negative (you won't be late = you will not be late). It is not a form of want, was or went — those verbs have their own negatives (doesn't want, wasn't, didn't go).

questions.prompt: Which sentence follows the comma rule of this chapter?

options.text: If the bus is late, I'll call you.
I'll call you, if the bus is late.
If, the bus is late I'll call you.
If the bus is late I'll call you,

questions.explanation: "If the bus is late, I'll call you." follows the rule: the if clause comes first, so a comma closes it before the result. "I'll call you, if the bus is late." adds a comma where none is needed, because the main clause comes first; the comma never goes straight after "If", and never at the end of the sentence.
